title: Instabilities of the continuous superradiant laser
authors: Bruno Laburthe-Tolra, Martin Robert-de-Saint-Vincent, Benjamin Pasquiou
abstract: We investigate the intensity stability of the superradiant laser. Our study focuses on the architecture where a continuous beam of atoms in an electronically excited state crosses the mode of a high-finesse Fabry-Perot cavity, which has been proposed as a new architecture of an active optical clock. We show that such superradiant laser can become unstable and develop chaotic behavior. We derive an analytical criterion for this instability and find that it may only occur when the lifetime of photons in the cavity is significantly shorter than the lifetime of atoms. This criterion allows for refining the necessary parameters to run a superradiant laser as a frequency reference in the optical domain. In particular, we point-out the consequences of the instability on intensity fluctuations and laser linewidth. On the other hand, we also point out that the superradiant laser, when in the unstable regime, can become an interesting playground for studying chaos. At the mean-field level, there is a direct mapping to the Bénard instability associated with fluid turbulence; however quantum fluctuations associated with photon out-coupling and atom re-filling substantially modify the expected behaviors. Finally, we point-out the existence of a regular self-pulsing regime at large atom numbers.
summary: The paper rigorously investigates the stability boundaries of a superradiant laser operating in an atomic cavity. It demonstrates that while the system can enter chaotic regimes analogous to fluid turbulence, these instabilities severely degrade its performance as a frequency reference due to phase drift. However, the authors also map out conditions for stable, regular self-pulsing oscillations, offering pathways to control this complex quantum optical system.
main_problem: The study investigates the intensity stability of a superradiant laser, determining the conditions under which it remains stable for use as an active optical clock versus when it develops chaotic behavior.
main_result: The superradiant laser can become unstable and exhibit chaotic dynamics when the photon lifetime is significantly shorter than the atomic lifetime ($\kappa > 4\Gamma_R$ and $N > N^*_c$). However, a regular self-pulsing regime exists at very large atom numbers.
method: The authors employed mean-field approximations, linear stability analysis (eigenvalue calculation), Monte Carlo simulations, and mapping the dynamics to known chaotic systems like the Lorenz model.
model_or_system: The system models a continuous beam of atoms in an electronically excited state interacting with a high-finesse Fabry-Perot cavity. The dynamics are governed by coupled rate equations for the cavity field and atomic coherences, incorporating photon loss ($\kappa$) and atomic decay rates ($\Gamma_R$).

important_parameters: The ratio of cavity loss rate to atomic decay rate ($\kappa$ vs $4\Gamma_R$), the critical atom numbers ($N_c, N^*_c$), and the relative timescales between photon and atomic lifetimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily relies on mean-field approximations. Furthermore, advanced fluctuation analyses required assuming Gaussian white noise or using specific time-coarse-graining techniques that break down in certain regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition from stable (low $\kappa$) to unstable/chaotic dynamics (high $\kappa$), showing intensity oscillations and phase drift. Later figures compare analytical models of self-pulsing against numerical simulations, confirming regular periodic behavior under specific conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the mean-field model and identifying instability criteria ($\kappa > 4\Gamma_R$). It then analyzes the resulting chaotic dynamics, comparing them to turbulence theory. Finally, it refines the analysis by calculating linewidths using fluctuation theories (TWA) and identifying a separate, stable self-pulsing regime at large atom numbers.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges quantum optics (superradiance/lasing) with nonlinear dynamics (chaos theory). The detailed analysis of phase drift versus amplitude fluctuations provides crucial guidelines for engineering robust quantum sensors and clocks based on cavity QED systems.

Partially Pumped Collective Emitters.note: The investigation of superradiant laser dynamics inherently deals with collective emission from an atomic ensemble; the analysis of stability boundaries and self-pulsing regimes directly relates to controlling collective decay processes in a cavity setting.
